analysis.one_liner: Lets families crushed by medical bills keep their home and wipe out medical and student debts in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill would have let families crushed by medical bills keep up to $250,000 of home equity and erase medical and student debts in bankruptcy, but it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a family's medical bills pile up, current bankruptcy law forces them through a means test, requires credit counseling, lets them protect only a small amount of home equity, and makes student loans nearly impossible to erase. This bill would have created a separate track for people whose debts came from illness: they could have kept up to $250,000 in home value or a burial plot, skipped the means test and credit counseling, and discharged student loans. The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Families whose finances were destroyed by illness — either their own medical bills or those of a spouse, child, parent, or sibling they cared for. The bill covers people whose unpaid medical debt over three years exceeded the lesser of 10% of their income or $10,000, or who lost wages or a job because of disease, caregiving, or a public health emergency like COVID-19. For them, bankruptcy would stop forcing a repayment plan, stop requiring credit counseling, protect up to $250,000 of home equity or a burial plot, and let them erase student loans. Spouses of qualifying debtors are covered too [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: A 'medically distressed debtor' — someone whose unpaid medical bills exceeded the lesser of 10% of income or $10,000 over three years, who lost income or a job because of illness or caregiving, or whose spouse is in that situation — could keep up to $250,000 of value in their home, co-op, or burial plot through bankruptcy [S2][S3].

The bill exempts medically distressed debtors from the Chapter 7 means test and from the Chapter 13 repayment-plan rules, so families thrown into bankruptcy by illness could have their debts wiped out rather than being forced into multi-year repayment plans [S2][S3].

Medically distressed debtors would no longer have to complete the pre-bankruptcy credit counseling requirement, and they could discharge student loan debt that is normally nearly impossible to erase [S2][S3].
To guard against abuse, a debtor claiming this relief must file a statement of medical expenses and declare under penalty of perjury that the expenses were not incurred just to qualify [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Creditors who would have recovered less. Debt collectors and buyers holding medical debt, credit card and consumer lenders holding unsecured balances, and student loan creditors would collect less from medically distressed households. Waiving the means test and enlarging the home exemption also shifts some losses to other creditors of the same debtors [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Debt collectors, lenders, student loan creditors

drawbacks.text: The bill would let a medically distressed debtor exempt up to $250,000 in home equity in bankruptcy, which is many times larger than the standard federal homestead exemption; a family with significant home equity could keep it while other creditors absorb the loss, and those costs can be passed on to other borrowers through prices and interest rates [S3].

Waiving the Chapter 7 means test removes the income screen that normally routes higher-earning debtors into Chapter 13 repayment plans, so some debtors with substantial income could erase debts that current law would require them to repay [S3].
Allowing medically distressed debtors to discharge student loans shifts the cost of unpaid education debt to the federal government and other student loan borrowers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: medical debt is one of the most common reasons families file for bankruptcy, and the bill would have let those families keep a home and a burial plot while wiping out medical bills and, in some cases, student loans [S2][S3]. The main cost is that the $250,000 home exemption is far more generous than the standard federal bankruptcy exemption, so it could shield substantial home equity from creditors even for debtors who are not financially desperate, and waiving the means test removes the usual income screen. The written attestation and perjury penalty are a reasonable safeguard, but creditors would bear the burden of policing abuse [S3]. On balance the trade favors families in genuine medical distress over their creditors, and the safeguard provisions address the most obvious objection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: On February 2, 2021, the bill was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill attracted only its five Senate sponsors and no Republican support, so it lacked the votes it would have needed even if it had reached the floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collectors, credit card lenders, and student loan creditors are better off, because the current bankruptcy rules that let them pursue families' homes and unpaid medical and student debt remain in place. Families with overwhelming medical bills got no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors and lenders; no relief for families

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were Democrats or allied independents; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the bill never advanced beyond the committee referral.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and medical debt buyers
industries.note: The bill makes large amounts of medical debt dischargeable and lets debtors keep home equity that collectors could otherwise reach, shrinking what these firms can recover from distressed families. For ordinary people, medical debt collectors profit by chasing families already coping with illness.

Households in medical distress could complete a faster Chapter 7 discharge without the means test, wiping out unsecured balances these lenders hold. Lenders' interest in maximum repayment runs against distressed borrowers' need for a fresh start.

Medically distressed debtors could discharge student loans in bankruptcy, ending the near-absolute protection those debts currently enjoy. Borrowers gain a safety valve; loan holders lose collections.

The bill waives the mandatory pre-bankruptcy credit counseling session for medically distressed debtors, removing a required stop at these agencies. A minor effect, but the counseling industry's role as a bankruptcy gatekeeper would narrow.
